divergences.title: The board is native; Plane is not carried
divergences.Covers: CF-03; [01-product-definition.md](01-product-definition.md) §5.1 (views, modules); the decision recorded as settled in [15-open-decisions.md](15-open-decisions.md) (DESIGN §5.2 option C).
divergences.Legacy baseline: The operator steers on a Plane board and reads the pipeline in a second tool; the board's order cannot be written by API (BL-18, BL-14, BL-28).
divergences.Sortyard: One console over one store: board, list, filters, reorder by drag, keyboard or API (TRK-014, TRK-007, UI-003).
divergences.Not better on: breadth of project-management features; see DIV-38.

divergences.title: A typed task replaces the spec block, control labels and text marks
divergences.Legacy baseline: The spec is a fenced block in the description; release, queue status and routing are labels; state is also in `state.json`. Filings have been invisible for want of a label, and board and record have disagreed (BL-12, BL-24).
divergences.Sortyard: One task object with typed fields; queue status is a field changed in the same transaction as board state (TRK-002, TRK-004, TRK-009).
divergences.Not better on: nothing found; free-form labels remain for people.
divergences.Demonstration: TRK-002 AC4, TRK-004 AC5, TRK-009 AC3.

divergences.title: No side door into the queue
divergences.Legacy baseline: Items filed directly on boards with task release off bypass the ready rules and preflight; six such tasks were claimed into an unregistered build target (BL-08).
divergences.Sortyard: Every released task passes the same gates, however it was filed (RDY-010).
divergences.Not better on: filing an ad-hoc item takes one more check; a task that fails it is refused where today it would start.

divergences.title: One transactional store replaces the files, the SQLite database, the JSONL ledgers and the sync
divergences.Legacy baseline: State and history live in several stores with no common order, kept in step by a sync job; they have disagreed in production (BL-14, BL-24).
divergences.Sortyard: Postgres holds state, ledger and queue; every change writes its event in the same transaction; blobs go to one location (OBS-001, DEP-003).
divergences.Not better on: a database is now required where files sufficed; an operator can no longer read state with `cat`.

divergences.title: Scheduling and hand-offs on events replace polling passes
divergences.Covers: LP-034, LP-035, LP-036, LP-037; CF-12; [01-product-definition.md](01-product-definition.md) §5.3 (three-minute passes).
divergences.Legacy baseline: Everything happens at the next pass: 3 minutes for the driver, 5 for the sync. One exception aborts a pass; one failed read degrades it (BL-03, BL-04, BL-22).
divergences.Sortyard: Each item is reconciled on the event that concerns it, with a periodic full evaluation as a backstop; one snapshot for each decision; atomic, fenced claims (SCH-006, SCH-014, SCH-015, SCH-016, FLW-019).
divergences.Not better on: a pass log was easy to read end to end; the decision log (DIV-06) has to replace that.
divergences.Demonstration: SCH-006 AC1, SCH-014 AC3, SCH-015 AC3, SCH-016 AC3, FLW-019 AC1, FLW-019 AC2.

divergences.title: The scheduler explains itself
divergences.Legacy baseline: Why a task waits is a hand derivation; phase and slot use are in a file on a cluster volume (BL-09, BL-28).
divergences.Sortyard: Pickup Preview, reason codes, a decision log and phase visibility through API, CLI and console (SCH-008, SCH-010, REC-011).
divergences.Not better on: nothing found.
divergences.Demonstration: SCH-008 AC4, SCH-010 AC4, REC-011 AC2.

divergences.title: Rank comes from parent links only
divergences.Legacy baseline: Milestone rank also matches a task by id prefix, so text decides order (BL-28).
divergences.Sortyard: Rank follows the parent relation; the importer converts prefix matches into parent links once (SCH-003).
divergences.Not better on: a task named by convention but never linked gets no rank until someone links it; the importer's report lists them.

divergences.title: Tuning is live, audited data
divergences.Legacy baseline: Lanes change by commit; caps and thresholds are literals in three files and need a release (BL-10).
divergences.Sortyard: Every tunable is a policy key read at decision time, with history (SCH-011, DEF-005). On a locked installation the change still arrives by commit (DIV-09).
divergences.Not better on: nothing found for caps; for lanes on a locked installation the route is the same as today.

divergences.title: Definitions live in the database; a locked installation pulls them from Git
divergences.Covers: CF-06; OD-5; the "definitions sync controller" row of OD-3.
divergences.Legacy baseline: `repos.yaml` is read from a Git clone on every pass: a merged change is in force within one pass with no further step. A failed clone degraded a pass (BL-10, BL-22).
divergences.Sortyard: Versions in the database, with validation, history and export (DEF-002). A locked installation pulls its definitions from the configured Git source itself, by poll and webhook; the last valid version stays in force (DEF-003). The earlier draft relied on a CI job running `apply`, which was slower and less visible than the legacy pull; that design was dropped.
divergences.Not better on: a two-way synchroniser (edit in the console, written back to Git) is still not built; no legacy behaviour depends on one.

divergences.title: The controller does not depend on the API, and version skew never pauses delivery silently
divergences.Legacy baseline: The conductor is a client of the dispatcher's API and skips its pass on version skew; it skipped every pass for about 32 minutes on 2026-11-12 with no alarm (BL-08, BL-25).
divergences.Sortyard: The controller calls the domain layer in-process (API-002). Adjacent versions run side by side; only a schema outside the supported window idles the controller, visibly (REC-015).
divergences.Not better on: supporting the previous minor's schema and stage contract costs work at every release (DEP-007).

divergences.title: Workers reach mirrors over the network, not a shared volume
divergences.Legacy baseline: Mirrors and run directories are on one volume mounted by every Job, which needs one node or `ReadWriteMany` storage (BL-14, BL-23).
divergences.Sortyard: Read-only Git over HTTP from a mirror service, with commits returned to a staging namespace (EXE-009). The shared-volume mode stays available, and an installation keeps it if the benchmark does not show the network path at least as fast.
divergences.Not better on: possibly stage start time on a single node; that is what the benchmark decides.

divergences.title: The control plane is protected from its workers
divergences.Legacy baseline: Workers run with small requests and no quota or priority class (BL-28).
divergences.Sortyard: A worker namespace with ResourceQuota and LimitRange, requests on the control plane, an optional PriorityClass (EXE-020).
divergences.Not better on: a quota can refuse a stage that would have started; admission caps are sized to stay below it.

divergences.title: Work in flight can be stopped and steered
divergences.Legacy baseline: A running task cannot be cancelled; steering is a prose procedure; no revision is checked where side effects happen (BL-28).
divergences.Sortyard: Cancel a stage or a chain, edit a task mid-flight, with an epoch checked at the integrator and the API (EXE-022, REC-020, REC-021).
divergences.Not better on: nothing found.
divergences.Demonstration: EXE-022 AC1, REC-020 AC3, REC-021 AC3.

divergences.title: Stalls are bounded, found and healed in minutes
divergences.Legacy baseline: One flat 4-hour stall threshold; causes polled every 30 minutes; watches and a person find the rest. Recorded stalls ran 8 hours to two days (BL-05, BL-06).
divergences.Sortyard: Every phase bounded (REC-001); causes re-evaluated on the resolving event (REC-008); bounds from each phase's own history, a no-progress watchdog and an announced self-heal queue (REC-026).
divergences.Not better on: a bound learned from history can be wrong for a phase that changes character; the ceiling stays the legacy threshold.
divergences.Demonstration: REC-001 AC3, REC-008 AC4, REC-026 AC1.

divergences.title: Leader election replaces single-writer by `Forbid` and `Recreate`
divergences.Legacy baseline: One writer is guaranteed by CronJob concurrency and a `Recreate` rollout; interrupted work waits for the next pass (BL-25).
divergences.Sortyard: A leader with a fencing epoch that hands over on shutdown (REC-014).
divergences.Not better on: leader election is more machinery than a CronJob flag; the chaos test is what keeps it honest.

divergences.title: Scoped identities replace the shared board key and the proxy header
divergences.Legacy baseline: One board key is shared by the sync and the driver, and by inference by the filing tools; the console trusts a header that pods can forge; agents operate through scripts that need a cluster shell (BL-26, BL-20).
divergences.Sortyard: Roles, scoped tokens, sign-in that cannot be forged from inside the cluster, and curated tools for each role over MCP (IAM-008, IAM-002, MCP-002).
divergences.Not better on: more credentials to issue and rotate than one shared key; expiry is tracked by the product (IAM-005).
divergences.Demonstration: IAM-008 AC4, IAM-002 AC4, MCP-002 AC3.

divergences.title: A minted Git credential replaces the owner's personal token
divergences.Legacy baseline: The Git write credential is the owner's personal token in a cluster Secret, with an expiry tracked by hand (BL-26).
divergences.Sortyard: A GitHub App whose tokens are minted for one operation and one repository, readable only by the integrator (CRD-007).
divergences.Not better on: the App must be installed on each organisation, which is the owner's action; a long-lived App key is in the cluster.

divergences.title: Releases by chart and image replace the bundle, its size cap and the bespoke controller
divergences.Covers: LP-260, LP-262, LP-263, LP-264, LP-265, LP-266; [01-product-definition.md](01-product-definition.md) §5.5 (release controller).
divergences.Legacy baseline: Code ships as a size-capped bundle; merged was not released; a hand-maintained Role blocked a release; every rollout has 30 to 40 seconds of nothing listening; the revision is a cluster annotation (BL-11, BL-25, BL-28).
divergences.Sortyard: Releases only from CI, a development build for every merge, one identity for chart, image and version, a namespace-admin install, surge rollouts and work that survives them (QLT-024, DEP-020, DEP-002, DEP-009, DEP-010, API-014). The legacy guarantees are kept: exact-commit builds, digest pinning, no cluster credential in CI.
divergences.Not better on: the legacy controller pulls a release into the cluster by itself; Sortyard leaves that to the operator's GitOps tool (DEP-016).
divergences.Demonstration: QLT-024 AC2, DEP-020 AC2, DEP-002 AC3, DEP-009 AC1, DEP-010 AC1, API-014 AC3.

divergences.title: Fewer moving parts
divergences.Legacy baseline: A board installation, an API, CronJobs, a release controller, a health job, host crons and a tools pod (BL-14).
divergences.Sortyard: Three Deployments and Postgres; mirror refresh, credential sync and health checks are loops inside the controller, each registered with a freshness window (DEP-001, EXE-008, CRD-006, REC-017).
divergences.Not better on: a loop inside the controller shares its fate; the health checker runs apart from what it watches (REC-017).

divergences.title: A task's page is its pipeline
divergences.Legacy baseline: The ticket is in one tool and its runs in another (BL-18).
divergences.Sortyard: One timeline for each task, with its chain, stages, change request and checks (UI-004).
divergences.Not better on: nothing found.

divergences.title: Metrics and reports come from the ledger
divergences.Covers: LP-154, LP-281; [01-product-definition.md](01-product-definition.md) §5.2 (external dashboards), §5.4 (health summary item), §5.7 (Slack cards and reports).
divergences.Legacy baseline: A cost item and a health item are rewritten on each board; an agent writes throughput reports and Slack cards (BL-16, BL-27).
divergences.Sortyard: A metric catalogue over the ledger, dashboards in the console, a generated daily record, notifications by rule (OBS-004, OBS-006, OBS-009, OBS-013).
divergences.Not better on: an agent's report can comment and judge; a generated record only states. The operator's own agent can still write one over MCP.

divergences.title: An internal sweep replaces drift consolidation
divergences.Legacy baseline: A check compares four copies of the plan and files what disagrees, false items included (BL-24).
divergences.Sortyard: The copies do not exist; a daily sweep reports what can still drift inside one store (GRM-007).
divergences.Not better on: nothing found, provided no second copy of the plan is kept outside Sortyard; the one-source audit checks that (MIG-011).

divergences.title: New behaviour without a release of the control plane
divergences.Legacy baseline: A new check, sensor or workflow step is a change to the conductor's code and a release of its bundle (BL-11, BL-10).
divergences.Sortyard: Definitions applied as bundles, containers under a contract, and HTTP (EXT-001).
divergences.Not better on: behaviour that needs new code inside the scheduler is still a release.

divergences.title: Pull requests belong to their task; issues are not mirrored onto the board
divergences.Legacy baseline: The sync projects issues and pull requests onto the board as items (BL-21 for whether anyone acts on them).
divergences.Sortyard: A pull request is part of its task's timeline (TRK-017); one opened outside becomes a `review` task (FLW-014); issues are not copied.
divergences.Not better on: an issue filed on the Git host no longer appears on the board by itself.
divergences.If used: an issue-intake sensor files tasks from issues through the API (EXT-004), scheduled in MS5 (WP5.8) and demonstrated on the recorded items.

divergences.title: Intake is filing and shaping; there is no sentence-to-tasks request
divergences.Legacy baseline: The dispatcher accepts a "new request" in a sentence and decomposes it into tasks, with a landing step (BL-21 for use).
divergences.Sortyard: Intake agents file typed tasks and get a verdict (TRK-012, TRK-013); grooming shapes them (GRM-001).
divergences.Not better on: an operator who types a sentence into the console gets no tasks from it unless an agent is asked.
divergences.If used: the decomposition is delivered as an intake agent with the `intake` role (MCP-002), scheduled in MS5 (WP5.7) and demonstrated on the recorded requests.

divergences.title: The concierge and its approval cards are kept
divergences.Covers: LP-225; the "embedded concierge" row of OD-3; [01-product-definition.md](01-product-definition.md) §5.2.
divergences.Legacy baseline: The console has an embedded chat agent that answers from live state with citations and proposes actions a person approves; it is built, with journeys and end-to-end specs (BL-18, BL-20).
divergences.Sortyard: The same, as a client of the operator-agent tools with the operator's permissions, off until a model credential is configured (UI-026, IAM-012). The earlier draft cut it on the argument that the operator's own agent reaches the same data over MCP. That is a different tool, not a better one, and no measurement supported the cut.

divergences.title: Design-first chains and self-repair of the dispatcher are not shipped
divergences.Covers: LP-115; the "template workflows, design-first chains, chain self-repair" row of OD-3; [01-product-definition.md](01-product-definition.md) §5.5.
divergences.Legacy baseline: The dispatcher has design chains (design, dual review, approval, build, verify) with console views, and a self-repair that edits and redeploys the control plane. The conductor path does not call them (BL-21 for whether anything else does).
divergences.Sortyard: The engine can express such a workflow (FLW-017); none is in the default bundle. Changes to the control plane are tasks that Sortyard builds and CI releases (QLT-024, DLV-002).
divergences.Not better on: a design-first flow is not available out of the box.
divergences.If used: a design-first workflow is added to the estate bundle in MS5 (WP5.9) and its console views are met by the task page (UI-004). Self-repair is not carried in either case: its job is done by a task on Sortyard's own board, released by CI.

divergences.title: The experiment rig, the scorecard battery and the eval views stay outside the product
divergences.Covers: LP-116, LP-282; CF-23; the "eval runner, scorecard battery, eval grid, experiment rig" row of OD-3; [01-product-definition.md](01-product-definition.md) §5.2, §5.5.
divergences.Legacy baseline: An experiment rig shares the legacy control plane: corpus, treatments, compare and eval views, an advisory scorecard battery (BL-21 for use).
divergences.Sortyard: Not carried into the product. The rig is kept as its own deployment when the legacy control plane is retired, and archived only if the census shows no use (MIG-013).

divergences.title: Skills, context recipes, archetypes and roles are not objects
divergences.Covers: CF-05; the "archetypes, roles as objects, skills, context recipes" row of OD-3.
divergences.Legacy baseline: The conductor injects no skill and builds no recipe: a worker gets a fixed packet, the task text, findings, CI excerpts and a checklist, and reads the repository's own agent guide. Skill files reach a worker only through its image or the repository (CF-05; `grooming.py` excludes the method directories from inputs; `design_review.py` reads its checklist from a skill file).
divergences.Sortyard: The same: versioned packet templates and checklists (EXE-015), and a binding that fixes the packet, the commit and the image digest, and so everything a worker reads (EXE-001). The owner's intended-use statement lists skills among what a binding fixes; it does, through the image and the commit.
divergences.Why the cut stands: the objects exist only in DESIGN v6. Not building them removes four large corpus tasks and adds no behaviour the estate has.

divergences.title: The shipped workflow is the one that runs
divergences.Legacy baseline: The conductor runs build, code review, test-determinism review, design review for UI changes, and auto-merge. The owner's "Delivery lanes" overrides the older template workflows (CF-04).
divergences.Sortyard: `change` and `job`, with that review policy (FLW-002, FLW-003, FLW-005 to FLW-009).
divergences.Why the cut stands: the template workflows are not on the conductor path; shipping them would add behaviour the estate has overruled.

divergences.title: Plan-only items: the extension registry, the separate runner services, Proposals, the roadmap projection, the fork lane
divergences.Covers: CF-05, CF-10, CF-22, CF-23; the "extension registry", "Proposals" and "eval runner" rows of OD-3, and its scope exclusions (other Git hosts, a Docker Compose install, translations).
divergences.Legacy baseline: None of these exists in the estate. Extension is a code change (DIV-23); reviews and required checks are the gates; pull requests opened outside are adopted (FLW-014); governance is not a product feature. The estate runs on GitHub and Kubernetes, in English.
divergences.Sortyard: Three extension mechanisms (EXT-001); three workloads (DEP-001); reviews with declared absent states (FLW-009); provider-hosted CI for forks and governance files for the upstream project (QLT-013, QLT-042).
divergences.Why the cut stands: each is a part to build, run and secure with no legacy behaviour behind it. Counted: three extension mechanisms instead of six registry kinds and an SDK; three long-lived workloads instead of six. Revisit when an extension is asked for that the three mechanisms cannot express.

divergences.title: Plane is frozen at cutover and archived at the verdict, with a rehearsed way back
divergences.Covers: CF-16; OD-4; the "Plane outbound projection" row of OD-3; [01-product-definition.md](01-product-definition.md) §5.1.
divergences.Legacy baseline: Plane is the board. The owner's standing default of 2026-11-06 keeps it as a read-only projection for one milestone after a cutover (INTENDED-USE; BL-24 for what a second copy costs).
divergences.Sortyard: No projection. At cutover the Plane project is frozen with a pointer to Sortyard; it is archived read-only at the hypercare verdict. Rolling back replays what changed since the cutover from a rollback export, written by the cutover kit and not by Sortyard (MIG-009). The earlier draft rolled back from the frozen snapshot alone, which would have lost the work done since the cutover.
divergences.Not better on: rollback takes minutes where a live projection would make it a switch; anyone still reading Plane sees a frozen board.

divergences.title: Merging past a quarantined job stays as it is for the estate
divergences.Legacy baseline: With only quarantined flaky jobs failing, the approved head is merged with an admin merge, once for each head (JQ).
divergences.Sortyard: The same, as a policy that the estate bundle ships on. New installations get it off by default, which changes nothing for the estate (MRG-004). The earlier draft switched it off everywhere; that would hold changes that merge today, with nothing measured to set against it.

divergences.title: Estate rules ship as policy packs, switched on in the estate bundle
divergences.Legacy baseline: Premise rules (intended use, reference clones, access citations), production flips held until preconditions are met, and release verification with shield and revert are enforced for the estate's projects.
divergences.Sortyard: The same rules as optional packs and an integration, on in the estate bundle (RDY-009, RDY-014, DLV-003). Off by default only for strangers, who have no such estate.

divergences.title: Reality reconciliation keeps running as a sensor
divergences.Legacy baseline: Grooming compares task premises with a recorded product-state file and forces a fix task when they differ.
divergences.Sortyard: The estate keeps running the comparison, as a sensor that files tasks through the API (EXT-004). A built-in pack follows after 1.0 (GRM-008).

divergences.title: No record stands for work that can never run
divergences.Legacy baseline: A rejected verify records a blocked follow-up request in the dispatcher that nothing dispatches: an artefact of two schedulers (DRV §4; BL-21 for how many exist).
divergences.Sortyard: One scheduler; a rejected review opens a fix round in the same chain (FLW-010), and follow-ups are tasks in Backlog (TRK-018).
divergences.Not better on: nothing found.

divergences.title: Estate mechanisms beyond the pipeline stay watched
divergences.Legacy baseline: The mechanism check watches runners, certificates, backups and scheduled CI on three clusters.
divergences.Sortyard: They are not product features, and they keep being watched: external heartbeats and an observer integration (REC-018, MIG-012). Nothing is switched off before it is registered or assigned an owner.

divergences.title: Plane features that the tracker does not carry
divergences.Covers: [01-product-definition.md](01-product-definition.md) §5.1 (cycles, pages, estimates, the intake module, deploy boards, Plane's own agents, importers and integrations, guests and teams, custom properties, the notifications inbox, attachments).
divergences.Legacy baseline: These exist in the board the estate runs. The record shows no use of them in delivery: the driver, the sync and the operations documents read none of them (inference; BL-21 for the count).
divergences.Sortyard: A tracker with the fields delivery reads, a closed set of kinds, an owner list and an attention list (TRK-003, UI-007, OBS-014).
divergences.Not better on: a team that used the board as a general project tool would lose those features.
divergences.If used: each feature with a count above zero is scheduled before the board that uses it is cut over (attachments: TRK-019; saved views are already TRK-015), or its replacement is shown in the journeys of TRK-014 AC4.

divergences.title: History stays in the frozen snapshot; the baselines are loaded
divergences.Legacy baseline: Past runs, reviews and costs are in the dispatcher's ledger and on the board.
divergences.Sortyard: The record stays where it is, frozen and verified (MIG-001). The figures needed to compare — every baseline in section 2 — are loaded as reference series, so dashboards show the legacy line beside Sortyard's (MIG-016).

divergences.title: The method's templates, roles, skills, scripts and runbooks stay in meta-harness
divergences.Legacy baseline: meta-harness holds template workflows, roles, skills, the `dispatch`, `validate` and `emit` scripts, and operating runbooks. Task registers and STATUS.md were retired by the estate itself on 2026-11-08.
divergences.Sortyard: Does not replace the method repository. Every enforceable rule in it is mapped to a requirement, a policy or a recorded retirement before the first cutover (MIG-010); runbooks for the legacy system retire with it (MIG-011).

divergences.title: The improvement ledger
divergences.Legacy baseline: The measurement contract describes a record for each tuning intervention, with before and after values and a verdict (BL-21 for whether entries exist).
divergences.Sortyard: Deferred past 1.0. The scorecard records before and after for every measured criterion, and policy changes are audited (QLT-051, SCH-011).
divergences.Not better on: no single record ties a tuning change to its hypothesis and verdict.

divergences.title: The estate's execution setup is kept, as settings and images
divergences.Legacy baseline: Build, verify and proof stages can run a privileged container sidecar; proof workers are provisioned for each project (browsers, a systemd executor image); workers use subscription credentials only, with API keys unset (MH).
divergences.Sortyard: The same, as settings rather than defaults. The sidecar is a project setting that the cutover kit turns on where it is used today (EXE-016). The estate's proof images are worker images named by its harness profiles (EXE-012). The estate bundle's policy selects the subscription pool only (CRD-002, CRD-003). A new installation starts with an API key and no sidecar, which changes nothing for the estate.

requirements.title: Projects with keys and sequence numbers
requirements.statement:
A project has a short upper-case key (`ROVE`) and every task in it gets a monotonically increasing
sequence number; `KEY-N` is a stable, human-quotable identifier that resolves everywhere (API, CLI,
MCP, UI URL, commit trailers).
acceptance: AC1: `GET /v1/…/tasks/ROVE-12` and the opaque id return the same task.
AC2: Sequence numbers are never reused, including after cancel; concurrent creates never collide (tested with 50 parallel creates).
AC3: The key is unique per workspace and immutable after the first task exists.
requirements.source: Plane identifiers `ROVE-123` are how every doc, comment and PR body refers to work (driver §1, task-pickup §8).

requirements.title: One task object: tracker fields plus a typed spec
requirements.statement:
A task carries tracker fields (title, markdown body, state, priority, parent, blocked-by, rank,
labels, due date) and a typed spec (`kind`, `repo`, `outcome`, `acceptance[]`, `needs[]`,
decision fields, `inputs[]`, `builds_on[]`, `select`, `delivery`). There is exactly one copy of
each fact; the spec is not a YAML block inside the body.
acceptance: AC1: The JSON Schema for Task has `kind`, `repo`, `outcome`, `acceptance`, `needs`, `inputs`, `builds_on`; the current `spec/task.schema.json` (no `kind`, `repo` or `acceptance`) is superseded.

AC2: Importing a legacy item whose description holds a ```` ```task ```` block produces the same typed fields, with Plane's own fields winning where both exist (title, priority, parent, relations, due date).
AC3: Editing a field through UI, CLI or MCP changes the same stored value (one round-trip test per surface).

AC4: Demonstration (replay, MS2) — every item of the driven boards, and the recorded invisible filings (HARNESS-608, HARNESS-615 to HARNESS-618), go through the importer's dry run and the filing operation. Target: 100% of items yield the typed fields the legacy parser read, and 100% of the invisible filings are refused or returned with a non-visible verdict in the filing response itself. Floor: every invisible filing is reported in the filing response; the legacy system reported them only at a later sweep (BL-12).
requirements.source: task-ready "The task item" (field ownership table); conductor README "Plane tasks". Gap: the frozen schema drops `kind`/`repo`/`acceptance` that the live ready rules require.
requirements.baseline: The spec is a fenced `task` block inside the Plane description, beside Plane's own fields, with a field-ownership table to say which copy wins (task-ready "The task item"). A filing with a malformed block or a missing label is found only by the later filing sweep (BL-12).

measured.target: 100% of items yield the typed fields the legacy parser read, and 100% of the invisible filings are refused or returned with a non-visible verdict in the filing response itself.
measured.floor: every invisible filing is reported in the filing response; the legacy system reported them only at a later sweep (BL-12).

requirements.title: Task kinds
requirements.statement:
`kind` is a closed set that selects the workflow and the lifecycle: operator kinds `feature`,
`fix`, `deployment`, `decision`, `parent`, `job`; system kinds `triage`, `regression`,
`follow-up`, `review` (an adopted outside PR), `ship` (a stranded build), `condition` (a
system-raised alarm, REC-023).
acceptance: AC1: Creating a task with an unknown kind is refused with a problem-detail naming the allowed set.

AC2: Each kind declares its properties as data: `parent` and `decision` are not claimable, `job` opens no change request, and each kind names its required fields (the ready rules of RDY-001 check them from MS2).
AC3: System kinds can only be created by system principals (IAM-008); the creator and reason are on the task.
requirements.source: task-ready "Kinds"; driver §4 (ad-hoc jobs, triage, lock-in); conductor README "Plane sync" (`queue_adopt`, `unlanded_builds`).

requirements.title: Task states and reason-carrying transitions
requirements.statement:
Board states: `backlog` (held), `todo` (planned), `in_progress`, `in_review`, `done`,
`cancelled`. Queue status is a separate typed field, not a label: `unreleased`, `released`,
`claimed`, `parked` (with reason), `handed_back` (with reason and evidence), `needs_human`
(with routes). Every transition is a named action that records actor, time and reason.
acceptance: AC1: A task cannot be `parked` or `handed_back` without a non-empty reason; the reason is shown inline on board and detail.
AC2: `PATCH` never changes state or queue status; only action endpoints do (API-006).
AC3: The legal-transition table is data in the repo and is unit-tested one test per transition plus one per refused transition.
AC4: A task that is `todo` on the board and in flight in the queue cannot be represented: every action changes board state and queue status in one transaction (the claim itself is SCH-016).

AC5: Demonstration (chaos, MS3) — the claim, requeue and cancel scenarios run 10,000 times with a fault injected at a random point of the action. Target: zero runs end with board state and queue status in disagreement, with no repair step. Floor: zero disagreements once the controller has restarted; the legacy system recorded this disagreement in production (BL-24).
requirements.source: task-pickup §2a (state table), §conformance row 4 (HARNESS-256: board says Todo, record says claimed); labels `conductor`, `self-heal`, `needs-human` are today's queue status (driver §4).
requirements.baseline: Queue status is three Plane labels plus the conductor's `state.json`. The board can say Todo while the record says claimed, and such an item is skipped every pass with nothing showing it (task-pickup conformance row 4, HARNESS-256; BL-24).

measured.target: zero runs end with board state and queue status in disagreement, with no repair step.
measured.floor: zero disagreements once the controller has restarted; the legacy system recorded this disagreement in production (BL-24).

requirements.title: Hierarchy: parents and children
requirements.statement:
A task may have one parent of kind `parent`; nesting is allowed. A parent is Done when every
planned child is Done, and nested parents close in the same evaluation. A parent in Backlog holds
all its descendants.
acceptance: AC1: Closing the last open child closes the parent, and its parent. Target: in the same transaction. Floor: within 10 s.
AC2: Moving a parent to Backlog marks every descendant held (`parent in backlog`) and moving it back clears the mark; from MS2 the mark is the reason code `held: parent in backlog` (SCH-009).
AC3: A parent with an open child cannot be moved to Done by hand without an explicit `force` reason that is audited.
requirements.source: driver §3 `queue_ready` (parent close), 2026-11-01 release note (#204 nested parents close); task-ready "A Backlog parent releases no children".

measured.target: in the same transaction.
measured.floor: within 10 s.

requirements.title: Dependencies are relations, and only relations
requirements.statement:
`blocked_by` is a typed relation between tasks in the same workspace. Cycles are refused at write
time. A dependency known only from prose does not exist; preflight (RDY-006) flags prose that
reads like a gate.
acceptance: AC1: Creating a relation that closes a cycle is refused and names the cycle.
AC2: A task whose blockers are not all `done` shows `blocked by KEY-N`, listing each open blocker and its state; from MS2 that is the reason code `held: blocked by` (SCH-009).
AC3: Cancelling a blocker does not clear the block silently: its dependants show `blocker cancelled` until the relation is removed or replaced.
requirements.source: task-pickup §2 rule 3; task-ready preflight check 5 ("Prose-only gates do not exist"); CORPUS R2 (description-level dependencies are not dependencies).

requirements.title: Manual order is writable through the API
requirements.statement:
Top-level tasks in a project have a manual `rank`. Drag-and-drop in the UI, `sortyardctl task
move`, and the API all write the same rank. Rank is the delivery order the scheduler reads
(SCH-002).
acceptance: AC1: `POST …/tasks/{id}/rank {before|after: KEY-N}` reorders; the next list call returns the new order (the Pickup Preview follows it from MS2, SCH-008).
AC2: Every reorder writes a ledger event with actor, old position, new position and optional reason.
AC3: A new top-level task lands last and the filing response says so.

AC4: Demonstration (benchmark, MS1) — a scripted reorder of 40 top-level tasks through the API, the case the 2026-11-08 import needed. Target: one call per move, each shown by the next list call in under 1 s, with nobody dragging. Floor: the whole reorder is done through the API in under 5 s per move; the legacy order cannot be written by API at all (BL-28).
requirements.source: task-ready "Only a person dragging on the board can reorder (Plane's API does not write `sort_order`)"; 2026-11-08 release note (the import could not set starting order).
requirements.baseline: Plane's API does not write `sort_order`: only a person dragging on the board can reorder, and the 2026-11-08 import could not set a starting order (task-ready; release note 2026-11-08; BL-28).

measured.target: one call per move, each shown by the next list call in under 1 s, with nobody dragging.
measured.floor: the whole reorder is done through the API in under 5 s per move; the legacy order cannot be written by API at all (BL-28).

requirements.title: Priority tiers
requirements.statement:
Priority is one of `urgent`, `high`, `medium`, `low`, `none`. `urgent` is the rush lane
(SCH-005); there is no separate urgent flag.
acceptance: AC1: The schema has one field; the frozen `priority.tier` + `priority.urgent` pair is collapsed.
AC2: Sorting by priority uses rank `urgent 0, high 1, medium 2, low 3, none 4`.
requirements.source: `drive.py` `RANK`; spec NOTES ambiguity 4 (urgent: flag or tier?).

requirements.title: Labels are for people; flags are for the system
requirements.statement:
Free-form labels exist for filtering and have no effect on scheduling. Everything the system
acts on is a typed field or relation: release status, queue status, kind, routes, selection
override, origin.
acceptance: AC1: Adding or removing any label changes no system field or state and — from MS2 — no eligibility (property test over random labels).

AC2: Each legacy control label — `conductor`, `job`, `self-heal`, `needs-human`, `route:*`, `decision`, `follow-up`, `regression`, `red-main`, `task`, `PR` — has a typed field or relation that carries its meaning; the table is in the docs and is the one the importer uses (MIG-003).

AC3: Demonstration (replay, MS2) — every control-label combination found on the driven boards, and the recorded missing-label filings, are imported. Target: 100% map to typed fields, and a task that is eligible in every respect but one names that one in its verdict. Floor: no legacy control state is unrepresentable, and no task can be invisible for want of a label (BL-12).
requirements.source: driver §3–§4 (labels as control signals); HARNESS-608/615–618 (filings invisible because a label was missing).
requirements.baseline: The eleven control labels of AC2 carry release, queue status, routing and kind. A filing without the right label is invisible to pickup until the sweep reports it (driver §3–§4; HARNESS-608, HARNESS-615 to HARNESS-618; BL-12).

measured.target: 100% map to typed fields, and a task that is eligible in every respect but one names that one in its verdict.
measured.floor: no legacy control state is unrepresentable, and no task can be invisible for want of a label (BL-12).

requirements.title: Notes and one activity timeline
requirements.statement:
People and agents can add markdown notes to a task. Notes, system events (state changes,
decisions, stage results, stall notices) and audit entries appear on one ordered timeline per
task. Machine-readable facts are typed event payloads, not text conventions inside notes.
acceptance: AC1: `GET …/tasks/{id}/timeline` returns notes and events interleaved by ledger order, paginated both ways.

AC2: The legacy text marks (`Triage:`, `Regression:`, `Adopt:`, `Ship:`, `Select:`, `Blocking-cause:`, `Delivery:`, `Failure:`, `Builds on:`, `Vendor:`, `Decided:`) each have a typed home; none is parsed from free text at runtime.
AC3: A system notice of a given kind is posted once per condition, not once per pass (dedupe key on the event).
requirements.source: `drive.py` `MARK` regex and `conductor_line`; conductor README "Blocking causes", "Harness routing"; driver §4 "one comment on its Plane item".

requirements.title: Decisions
requirements.statement:
A decision task has a question, options, a recorded default, a `decide_by` time, a
`premise_class` flag and a route for whoever applies the answer. The model, the answer action
and the lifecycle (RDY-015) land together in MS2; in MS1 a decision is an ordinary task of kind
`decision`.
acceptance: AC1: A decision without `default` and `decide_by` is not ready and says why.
AC2: An answer is an explicit chosen value recorded through the answer action; a note is never an answer.
AC3: A decision never blocks a routine build: features are written against the default; only a premise-class decision may be a blocker.
requirements.source: task-ready rule 6; conductor README "Plane tasks" (explicit `Decided:` only; premise-class decisions never stand on a default).

requirements.title: File many tasks from one file
requirements.statement:
`sortyardctl task file <file>` and one API call file a set of tasks from a YAML document or a
markdown file of ```` ```task ```` blocks: dependencies first, ids already present updated in
place when their text changed, never duplicated.
acceptance: AC1: Filing the same file twice creates nothing the second time (idempotent by task `external_id`).
AC2: The call is atomic per file: a file with an unresolvable dependency files nothing and names it.

AC3: The response lists a result per task (created, updated, unchanged or failed, with the reason) and the command exits non-zero when any failed; from MS2 each result carries the filing verdict (TRK-013).
requirements.source: task-ready "File tasks with `plane_tasks.py file`"; conductor README "Filing visibility".

requirements.title: Filing verdicts: a filing is done when pickup can see it
requirements.statement:
Every task has a computed filing verdict: `VISIBLE`, `WILL-RELEASE`, `WAITING` (with each named
blocker), or `FAILED` (with the failed check). The verdict fails closed: an input that cannot be
read is `FAILED (read)`, never visible.
acceptance: AC1: The verdict is returned by create, by file-many, by `sortyardctl pickup status KEY-N` and on the task detail page.

AC2: A task that stays `WILL-RELEASE` longer than the release limit (default 30 minutes, the legacy sweep interval) becomes `FAILED (release)`; from MS5 it also appears on the project's single `FILING-INVISIBLE` condition (REC-023).
AC3: Verdict vocabulary and exit codes match `pickup_status.py`, so existing agent prompts keep working.
requirements.source: conductor README "Filing visibility"; task-pickup §9; HARNESS-251.

requirements.title: Board, list and filters
requirements.statement:
The tracker has a board view (columns by state), a list view, and filters on project, state,
kind, priority, label, parent, queue status and text. Filter, sort and selection live in the URL.
acceptance: AC1: A URL copied from one browser reproduces the same view in another.
AC2: Lists are server-paginated with cursors in both directions and show a total count.
AC3: System-raised tasks (TRK-003 system kinds) are visually distinct and filterable in one click.

AC4: Demonstration (benchmark, MS2) — the operator journeys of BL-18 (find a task, see the health items, see why a task waits, reorder a milestone, file and release a task) are scripted against Sortyard and against the legacy pair of Plane and the harness console, counting steps, tools and time. Target: every journey takes at most half the legacy steps, in one tool, with each view rendered in under 1 s. Floor: no journey takes more steps or more time than on the legacy pair, and none needs a second tool (BL-18).
requirements.source: harness-console journeys J2; Plane board usage (driver §6 "The owner steers in Plane").
requirements.baseline: The board is Plane, a separate product with its own database and services ([12-quality-bar.md](12-quality-bar.md) §1), and the pipeline is shown by a second tool, the harness console; the owner steers in one and reads the other (driver §6 "The owner steers in Plane"; BL-18, BL-14).

measured.target: every journey takes at most half the legacy steps, in one tool, with each view rendered in under 1 s.
measured.floor: no journey takes more steps or more time than on the legacy pair, and none needs a second tool (BL-18).

requirements.title: Saved views
requirements.statement: An operator can save a filter set under a name, per user or shared with the workspace.
acceptance: AC1: A saved view is an API object; the UI is a client of it.
AC2: Deleting a shared view is audited.
requirements.source: Plane saved views (DESIGN §5.2 option C: concepts taken, not code).

requirements.title: Bulk edit
requirements.statement: Select many tasks and change state, priority, labels or parent in one audited operation.
acceptance: AC1: A bulk change of N tasks is one request, N ledger events, one audit entry linking them.
AC2: A bulk change that would break an invariant for any task applies to none and names the offenders.
requirements.source: the 2026-11-08 import and the queue audits were bulk operations done by script.

requirements.title: Links
requirements.statement:
A task has typed links: pull requests, commits, CI runs, other tasks, external URLs. Links
created by the system (the PR a chain opened) are facts with an observed-at time.
acceptance: AC1: A task's PR link shows state (open, merged, closed) as last observed, with the observation time.
AC2: An internal-only URL is labelled as such when rendered into anything a worker will read (EXE-015).
requirements.source: `pr_body` incident note (workers followed a tailnet-only Plane link and reported missing evidence).

requirements.title: Follow-up items never enter the queue by themselves
requirements.statement:
Follow-ups from reviews are created in Backlog at low priority, unreleased, linked to the PR and
the originating task; one item per approval, deduplicated across rounds.
acceptance: AC1: A follow-up is never claimed until a person or grooming moves it to Todo and releases it.
AC2: A review that lists the same finding in two rounds produces one follow-up.
AC3: Filing survives a tracker write failure: queued on the chain record and retried every reconcile.

AC4: Demonstration (count, MS4) — after the delivery scenario suite, count the records that stand for work but can never run: requests or stages that are neither terminal, nor owned by a live chain, nor a task on the board. Target: zero, with no such state in the schema. Floor: zero; the usage census counts the blocked follow-up requests that rejected verifies left in the legacy dispatcher (BL-21).
requirements.source: driver §4 (reviewing); TEST-REVIEW "Review scope" (PRE-EXISTING → follow-ups, `retry_test_follow_ups`).

measured.target: zero, with no such state in the schema.
measured.floor: zero; the usage census counts the blocked follow-up requests that rejected verifies left in the legacy dispatcher (BL-21).

requirements.title: File attachments
requirements.statement:
Binary attachments on tasks are out of scope for 1.0, on the evidence that links cover the
estate's use. The cut is conditional: if the usage census (MIG-017) counts attachments in use on
a driven board, this requirement is scheduled before that board's cutover.
acceptance: AC1: The schema reserves no attachment field in v1; adding one later is an additive API change.
requirements.source: inference — no attachment use found in the conductor, plane-sync or the operations docs.

requirements.title: Ready rules check the task's shape
requirements.statement:
A task is ready when: it names one registered repo and one single-sentence outcome; its
acceptance entries are named tests (`test` + `name`) or journeys; parent and blockers resolve in
the same project; priority is valid; a `deployment` lists its `needs`; a `decision` has a default
and `decide_by`. Required fields per kind follow task-ready's table.
acceptance: AC1: Each rule has an id and a message; `GET …/tasks/{id}/readiness` lists every failing rule.
AC2: Whether acceptance is required is policy data per project (`ready.require_acceptance`, default `true` for `feature` and `fix`) — see open decision OD-10.
AC3: A feature whose text names a deploy, production, real accounts, credentials or owner sign-off fails rule `placement` and is told to split into a `deployment` or `decision`.
requirements.source: task-ready "Ready rules" 1–6 and "Kinds"; AGENTS.md "Delivery lanes" rule 6.

requirements.title: Sizing lints are warnings
requirements.statement:
The "one PR's worth" rules that can be checked mechanically run as warnings that never change
readiness: more than three acceptance tests, "and" joining two results in the outcome, a title
with more than one verb/object.
acceptance: AC1: Warnings are returned next to the verdict and shown on the task; they are never errors.
AC2: False positives are expected: there is no way to turn a warning into a hold without a policy change.
requirements.source: task-ready "One PR's worth" (rules 2–4 as `warn:`).

requirements.title: Release happens once
requirements.statement:
The system releases a ready `feature`, `fix` or `deployment` in Todo exactly once. If a person
withdraws the release, it stays withdrawn until a person releases it again.
acceptance: AC1: A task un-released by an operator is never re-released by the system (tested across restarts and upgrades).
AC2: The release event records which rules and checks passed and their versions.
requirements.source: task-pickup §2 rule 5 ("taking the label off sticks").

requirements.title: Release conditions
requirements.statement:
Release requires: ready (RDY-001); every blocker Done; parent not in Backlog; `repo` belongs to
the project; preflight passed (RDY-005); the project has release switched on. The evaluation
reads one consistent snapshot.
acceptance: AC1: With release switched off for a project, decisions and parents still run their lifecycle and nothing is released.
AC2: A failure to evaluate one task (bad data) holds that task with a reason and never stops others.
requirements.source: task-pickup §2; driver §1 (`tasks: on|off`).

requirements.title: Preflight: named checks against live surfaces
requirements.statement:
Before release, every applicable preflight check must pass against the surface the build will
really use. A check that cannot run is `unverifiable` and holds the task exactly like a failure.
A held task stays visible in Todo, unreleased, with one notice naming each failed check and its
fix; a new notice appears only when the set of failing checks changes.
acceptance: AC1: Each check has a stable id, an owner (who fixes it) and a fix hint; results are stored per task with the time and the evidence read.
AC2: No check reads a parallel store or a cache of the thing it verifies.
AC3: Preflight re-runs when the task, the project config or a relevant integration changes, and at claim time (SCH-017).
requirements.source: task-ready "De-risking: the preflight gate"; conductor README "Preflight"; the 2026-11-09 Sortyard stall (six tasks claimed into an unregistered build target).

requirements.title: The v1 preflight checks
requirements.statement:
Checks shipped in 1.0, with the legacy ids kept: `build-target` (repo registered and mirrored),
`write-reach` (the landing credential can push), `evidence-reach` (the worker can read what its
job needs), `inputs` (every cited file exists in a repo the build checks out; no workspace
paths), `needs` (each named secret or resource exists — presence only, never values),
`dependency-graph` (anything the text treats as a gate is a relation), `placement` (nothing needs
a live third party mid-build), `checker-cases` (detector tasks enumerate must-catch/must-allow),
`wide-invariant` (a claim over "every X" names its list; more than 8 surfaces → split).
acceptance: AC1: `build-target`, `inputs` (path form), `dependency-graph`, `placement`, `checker-cases`, `wide-invariant` work with no Git host configured (MS2); `write-reach`, `evidence-reach`, `inputs` (existence), `needs` run against the Git host adapter (MS4, WP4.9).
AC2: Each check has a fixture set replayed in CI; the legacy `queue_audit.py --fixtures` cases are imported as fixtures.
AC3: `checker-cases` and `wide-invariant` mark the task for shaping rather than leaving it plainly held; shaping consumes the mark from MS5 (GRM-006).
requirements.source: conductor README "Preflight" checks 1–9; task-ready preflight 1–8.

requirements.title: Needs are routed to whoever can meet them
requirements.statement:
Each `need` has a description and a route: `devops`, `owner` or `agent` (default `devops`). A
task held only by needs is `needs_human` with its routes. `owner` creates a linked decision;
`agent` queues a linked job with the step and its completion check. Removing a met need
re-evaluates release.
acceptance: AC1: The "routed to me" list for each route is one API call and one UI view.
AC2: A need is discharged by an explicit action recording who, when and the verification reference.
AC3: With all needs met, a ready task is released on the next evaluation without anyone touching it again.
requirements.source: k3s driver "Discharging needs and decisions"; HARNESS-247.

requirements.title: Outcome already met
requirements.statement:
When discharging a deployment's needs delivered its whole outcome, the task closes Done on a
recorded, non-empty verification instead of being built.
acceptance: AC1: `outcome_met.verification` must name the check and what it established; an empty value is refused.
AC2: The task closes as the same item (no duplicate), keeping the verification on its timeline.
requirements.source: k3s driver "Discharging needs and decisions" (`outcome_met`); HARNESS-272.

requirements.title: Premise rules as an optional policy pack
requirements.statement:
The estate's premise rules ship as a policy pack, switched on in the estate bundle and off by
default for new installations: `intended_use` recorded as consistent/contradicts;
reference-clone quarantine (capabilities taken, business shape not taken or imported by a
premise-class decision); access tasks cite a decision that decides that specific target.
acceptance: AC1: With the pack enabled, a task whose milestone contradicts the project's intended-use record is not ready, and neither is anything under it.
AC2: A citation of a decision that decides a different question raises one `CITATION-MISMATCH` condition routed to the owner, never duplicated.
AC3: The pack is data plus checks registered in the preflight framework; core has no NonceLogic-specific wording.
requirements.source: conductor README "Plane tasks" (intended use, reference clones, access citations; grounding cases A05-D1, Loopmentum/Okara).

requirements.title: No side door into the queue
requirements.statement:
A task created directly as released (the legacy `add_item.py` path) passes the same ready and
preflight gates as a planned task. There is no project setting that bypasses them.
acceptance: AC1: `sortyardctl task add --release` on a task that fails preflight returns `FAILED (preflight …)` and leaves it unreleased.
AC2: Ad-hoc `job` tasks run the checks that apply to jobs (`build-target`, `evidence-reach`, `inputs`).

AC3: Demonstration (parity, MS2) — the six recorded tasks of 2026-11-09 and the HARNESS-504 case are filed with `task add --release` into a project whose build target is not registered. Target: 100% are refused at filing with the failing check named, and none is released. Floor: none becomes claimable in the Pickup Preview; the legacy system claimed all six (BL-08).
requirements.source: task-ready ("directly-filed items on `tasks: off` boards bypass even the ready rules", HARNESS-504).
requirements.baseline: Items filed directly on boards with task release off bypass the ready rules and preflight (task-ready, HARNESS-504). On 2026-11-09 six tasks on such a board were claimed into a build target that was not registered (BL-08).

measured.target: 100% are refused at filing with the failing check named, and none is released.
measured.floor: none becomes claimable in the Pickup Preview; the legacy system claimed all six (BL-08).

requirements.title: Retroactive queue audit
requirements.statement:
One command re-runs ready and preflight over everything already released or planned and reports
per project; with `--apply` it withdraws release from failing items with one notice each. It
never releases anything.
acceptance: AC1: The report is deterministic and diff-able between runs.
AC2: `--fixtures` writes each failure as a replayable preflight fixture.
requirements.source: conductor README "Retroactive audit" (`queue_audit.py`, COND-505).

requirements.title: A hand-back owes a check or a gap
requirements.statement:
Resolving a hand-back requires recording either the preflight check that would have caught it or
a process-gap task explaining why it cannot be checked.
acceptance: AC1: The self-heal resolution action refuses to close without `preventable_by` (a check id or a task reference).
AC2: A monthly report lists hand-backs by `preventable_by`.
requirements.source: task-ready ("every hand-back owes one of two things in the same pass that returns it").

requirements.title: One bad project config never stops the others
requirements.statement:
Project configuration is validated entry by entry. An invalid entry is dropped for that
evaluation and marks the project `config-invalid`, naming the rule it breaks (from MS5 as one
`CONFIG-INVALID <project>` condition, REC-023); every other project runs normally.
acceptance: AC1: Injecting an invalid config for one project leaves the claims of the others unchanged (replay test).
AC2: The mark clears only when that project's config validates.
requirements.source: conductor README "Product configuration failsafe" (2026-11-10).

requirements.title: Estate preconditions for production flips
requirements.statement:
A task that flips production cannot be released until the estate facts it assumes are named
blockers or needs and are discharged; urgency alone never exempts it.
acceptance: AC1: A production-flip task with an undischarged precondition is ineligible even when `urgent`.
AC2: The verification dependency stays on the task after the need is removed, so the evidence survives.
requirements.source: conductor README "Plane sync" `cutover_readiness`; `gate_cutover_pickup` note ("Urgency alone cannot exempt a plan-backed production flip"); DESIGN §3.7b (HARNESS-274).

requirements.title: Decision lifecycle
requirements.statement:
An unanswered routine decision takes its default at `decide_by`: a notice, then Done. An answered
decision stays open, routed to whoever applies the answer. A premise-class decision never takes
its default: past `decide_by` it is escalated once to the owner list and stays open. A decision
recorded as decided closes on the next evaluation.
acceptance: AC1: Time-travel test: one tick after `decide_by` a routine decision is Done with a "default applied" event; a premise-class one is `needs_human` routed to `owner`.
AC2: The answer is re-read from the store at every evaluation; nothing is trusted from a cache.
AC3: Work blocked by a premise-class decision is never released while it is undecided.
requirements.source: conductor README "Plane tasks"; task-pickup §2 table; LOOP-632 and LOOP-DEC-FIRST-CUSTOMER grounding cases.

requirements.title: An empty eligible queue with known work is a defect
requirements.statement:
When a project's eligible queue is empty and known work exists (unshaped milestones, recorded
findings, tripwire items), the system starts a grooming run for that project.
acceptance: AC1: With the queue emptied in a fixture, a grooming run is dispatched within one evaluation; with no known work, none is dispatched.
AC2: New observations arriving during a run stay pending for the next run.
requirements.source: conductor README (grooming process step); DESIGN §3.5 ("never an empty groomed queue").

requirements.title: Grooming runs on the frontier model, or says so
requirements.statement:
Grooming's judgment runs on the model the policy names. A result from another model is rejected
before anything is filed, except a fallback the system itself stamped because no eligible
account existed; the stamp is kept on the run and its receipt.
acceptance: AC1: A result whose recorded actual model differs from policy, without a system fallback stamp, files nothing and the run is marked failed with that reason.
AC2: The model rule is policy data (`grooming.model`, `grooming.accept_stamped_fallback`).
requirements.source: conductor README (grooming: "rejects a missing or non-Opus actual-model receipt … except a Codex result that MH stamped as the model-fallback move").

requirements.title: Grooming output is validated before it reaches the board
requirements.statement:
The validator rejects: missing hindsight citations, repeated root causes, unready builds, builds
gated on routine decisions, dependency cycles, edits to existing tasks, report-only results, and
a no-work disposition for an input that requires work. Every new task must be `VISIBLE` or
`WAITING` on named board work.
acceptance: AC1: Each rejection reason has a fixture; a rejected run files nothing.
AC2: A plan-caused pickup failure triggers one repair run restricted to the ids it filed; filed ids are corrected in place, never duplicated.
AC3: A lost response is recovered by id from the store; the same input never files twice.
requirements.source: conductor README (grooming validation, repair, `grooming.json` recovery).

requirements.title: Grooming inputs and their bookkeeping
requirements.statement:
Inputs are finished findings runs, findings documents, tripwire items and stale premises, each
identified by content hash. An input is consumed only when its disposition is recorded
(`filed`, `covered:<task>`, `no-work:<why>`). Packets fill newest-first to the size cap; what
does not fit is deferred, never dropped.
acceptance: AC1: An over-budget packet defers inputs and still dispatches; it is never a terminal failure.
AC2: The run record holds dispatch identity, inputs, phase, filed ids and per-task pickup evidence.
requirements.source: conductor README (grooming packets, 200,000-character limit, `grooming.json`).

requirements.title: Grooming silence raises an alarm
requirements.statement:
After two consecutive failed grooming attempts, or an eligible queue empty for longer than the
limit with no run dispatched (default 60 minutes, the legacy value), one `GROOMING-STALLED
<project>` condition is raised with the error, attempt count, queue-empty-since time and the
pickup status of every open planned task.
acceptance: AC1: The condition is updated in place, never duplicated, and closes when the project has an eligible head again.
AC2: Both thresholds are policy data.
requirements.source: conductor README ("Silence is the defect").

requirements.title: Shaping turns an unready task into ready ones
requirements.statement:
A task that fails readiness or the sizing checks goes to shaping: one agent run, no reviews, that
produces ready children, decisions and deployment tasks under the same parent, keeping the
original id for the first piece.
acceptance: AC1: The driver never fills gaps itself: an unready task is never dispatched to a build.
AC2: Split ids follow `X-F3`, `X-F3b`, `X-F3c`; later pieces depend on earlier ones only where stated.
requirements.source: task-ready ("The driver never fills gaps itself"; "One PR's worth" rules 5–6).

requirements.title: Internal consistency sweep replaces drift consolidation
requirements.statement:
A daily sweep reports what can still drift inside one store: duplicate tasks, Done parents with
open children, Done tasks with open PRs they own, open failure items with no recorded reason.
Each finding is one deduplicated condition.
acceptance: AC1: The plan↔board↔STATUS.md↔register comparisons of `drift.py` have no equivalent because those copies no longer exist; the sweep's scope is documented as exactly the list above.
AC2: A sweep whose read fails reports failure and is retried; it never reports "clean".

AC3: Demonstration (count, MS5) — the copies of plan state that can disagree are counted, and the sweep runs over the boards imported for the pilot rehearsal. Target: zero second copies and zero false findings. Floor: fewer copies than the legacy four, and fewer false findings than the legacy check filed on the same boards (BL-24).
requirements.source: conductor README "Drift consolidation" and `queue_reconciliation`; HARNESS-249.
requirements.baseline: The legacy sync compares four copies of the plan — plan file, board, STATUS.md and registers — and files what disagrees; on a board that has no plan file by design it filed false items (conductor README "Drift consolidation"; SORTYARD-68, SORTYARD-69; BL-24).

measured.target: zero second copies and zero false findings.
measured.floor: fewer copies than the legacy four, and fewer false findings than the legacy check filed on the same boards (BL-24).

requirements.title: Reality reconciliation
requirements.statement:
Comparing task premises against a recorded product-state file (connected sites, live
installations) and forcing a fix task on divergence is kept as an estate policy pack after 1.0.
acceptance: AC1: Until it ships, the estate keeps running the comparison as a sensor that files tasks through the API (EXT-004).
requirements.source: conductor README (grooming `reality:` observations; Joe 2026-11-06).

requirements.title: One definition of eligible
requirements.statement:
A task is eligible when all hold: its project has build switched on; it is released (RDY-003);
board state is `todo`; it has no live chain; its kind is claimable; claim-time gates pass
(SCH-017). One function computes this; the Pickup Preview, the scheduler and the filing verdict
all call it.
acceptance: AC1: There is exactly one implementation of eligibility in the codebase (import-graph test: preview, scheduler and verdict share it).
AC2: For every ineligible task the function returns at least one reason code from the catalogue (SCH-009).
requirements.source: task-pickup §4 "Eligible"; CORPUS M1.10 (Pickup Preview and conductor are clients of one evaluator).

requirements.title: Pickup order is a total order
requirements.statement:
Within a project, eligible tasks are ordered by: (1) `urgent` first; (2) milestone rank —
the position of the task's top-level ancestor in the project's manual order, tasks with no
planned ancestor after all planned work; (3) priority (`high`, `medium`, `low`, `none`);
(4) sequence number ascending. No ties remain.
acceptance: AC1: Golden tests reproduce the worked derivation in task-pickup §8 (CPV2-574) from fixture data.
AC2: The key list is policy data (`prioritization.keys`), defaulting to the order above; weighted scoring is not offered.
AC3: A project with no planned top-level tasks orders by priority then sequence.
requirements.source: task-pickup §4; driver §4 "Pickup"; DESIGN §3.5 (lexicographic, no weights).

requirements.title: Milestone rank comes from the parent chain
requirements.statement:
A task's milestone rank is found by walking its parent relation to the top-level task. The
legacy fallback that matches a task id by text prefix (`BV-15-F2` ranks with `BV-15`) is applied
only by the importer, which converts prefix matches into parent links.
acceptance: AC1: The scheduler contains no title or id string matching.
AC2: The importer's report lists every task ranked by prefix and the parent link it created for it.

AC3: Demonstration (replay, MS2) — the recorded passes are replayed with rank taken from parent links only, after the importer has converted prefix matches. Target: 100% of recorded claim orders are reproduced, with every prefix-ranked task linked to its parent by the importer and none left for a person. Floor: no divergence in the replay comparison (MIG-005) is caused by rank, and renaming a task changes no rank, which it can under the legacy rule (BL-28).
requirements.source: `milestone_rank` (task-pickup §4 step 2: "equals its task id … or a prefix of these followed by `-`").
requirements.baseline: `milestone_rank` also ranks a task whose id is a text prefix of a top-level task's (task-pickup §4 step 2). Inference from that rule: renaming a task can change its rank (BL-28).

measured.target: 100% of recorded claim orders are reproduced, with every prefix-ranked task linked to its parent by the importer and none left for a person.
measured.floor: no divergence in the replay comparison (MIG-005) is caused by rank, and renaming a task changes no rank, which it can under the legacy rule (BL-28).

requirements.title: Lanes: slots per project
requirements.statement:
Each project has `lanes`: the most non-urgent chains it may have in flight. A slot is held from
claim until the chain is done, parked, handed back or `awaiting-deployment`. `lanes: 0` pauses
the project. Projects do not compete for each other's lanes.
acceptance: AC1: With `lanes: 2` and three eligible tasks, exactly two are claimed; the third shows `held: lanes full (2/2)` naming the two holders and their phases.
AC2: An in-flight task in phase `merging` still holds its slot; one in `awaiting-deployment` does not.
AC3: Changing `lanes` takes effect at the next evaluation without a restart (SCH-011) and is audited.
requirements.source: task-pickup §4 "Slots", §5; driver §1 (`lanes`); k3s driver "Running-system delivery" (awaiting-deployment releases the build slot).

requirements.title: The rush lane
requirements.statement:
An `urgent` task is claimed in addition to the project's lanes, never instead of a claimed task,
and never preempts a running stage. Its stages run at rush priority and use the reserved heavy
slot (SCH-007).
acceptance: AC1: With lanes full, an urgent task is still claimed at the next evaluation.
AC2: From MS3: no running Job is deleted or deprioritised because an urgent task arrived.
AC3: Urgent tasks in flight are not counted in lane occupancy.
requirements.source: driver §4 ("Urgent runs as a harness `rush` request and ignores the lane limit"); task-pickup §3 ("Nothing preempts a claimed item").

requirements.title: A freed slot is reused promptly
requirements.statement: When a slot frees, the next eligible task is claimed on that event, not at the next fixed pass.
acceptance: AC1: Demonstration (benchmark, MS3) — the scenario suite measures the time from a slot-free event to the next claim event over 1,000 hand-overs. Target: p95 at most 5 s. Floor: p95 at most 30 s and maximum at most 120 s; the legacy minimum is one pass, up to 180 s (BL-04).
AC2: A periodic full re-evaluation (default every 60 s) guarantees progress even if an event is missed.
requirements.source: task-pickup §3 ("Minimum latency from 'slot freed' to 'next item claimed' is one pass" — three minutes today).
requirements.baseline: A freed slot is reused at the next pass, and passes run every three minutes (task-pickup §3; BL-04).

measured.target: p95 at most 5 s.
measured.floor: p95 at most 30 s and maximum at most 120 s; the legacy minimum is one pass, up to 180 s (BL-04).

requirements.title: Stacked admission caps for heavy stages
requirements.statement:
Stage classes are `light` (shape) and `heavy` (build, verify, proof). Heavy stages start only
within three caps, all policy data: a cluster heavy cap, a train cap for non-rush work (the
difference is reserved for rush), and a per-project heavy cap that rush ignores. Among admissible
stages, rush goes first, then creation order.
acceptance: AC1: With caps 4 / 3 / 2, a fourth non-rush heavy stage waits with reason `throttled: train heavy cap (3/3)`; a rush stage still starts.
AC2: Work that cannot be admitted is never launched to fight for resources: no Job exists for it.
AC3: Defaults are documented by node size (DEP-021); the chart default is cluster 2 / train 1 / project 1.
requirements.source: `mh.py` `caps_allow`, `_drive_order`; driver §5 "Capacity knobs" (`MH_HEAVY_CAP`, `MH_TRAIN_HEAVY_CAP`, `MH_PROJECT_HEAVY_CAP`).

requirements.title: Pickup Preview
requirements.statement:
For any project the system answers: the current queue in claim order, the reason code(s) for
every task that is not claimable now, who holds each slot and in what phase, and a simulation of
the next N claims (default 10). Available through API, CLI (`sortyardctl queue`, `why KEY-N`),
MCP and UI.
acceptance: AC1: The preview is computed by the same function the scheduler runs, from the same snapshot type.
AC2: The time from changing a lane cap, a priority, a rank or a dependency to the preview showing it. Target: 1 s. Floor: 5 s.
AC3: Every place an item can wait (task-pickup §7's table) corresponds to a reason code shown here.

AC4: Demonstration (benchmark, MS2) — for each place an item can wait in task-pickup §7's table, a scripted operator asks why a task is not running. Target: one call or one screen answers in under 1 s for 100% of the places. Floor: every place is answered in fewer steps than the legacy route, which needs `state.json` from the cluster or a hand derivation (BL-09).
requirements.source: task-pickup §7 ("Where a reader sees it": several rows say "Not visible"); HARNESS-251, HARNESS-256.
requirements.baseline: Several of the places an item can wait are "Not visible" to a reader (task-pickup §7); phase and slot use are in `state.json` on a cluster volume (HARNESS-251, HARNESS-256; BL-09).

measured.target: one call or one screen answers in under 1 s for 100% of the places.
measured.floor: every place is answered in fewer steps than the legacy route, which needs `state.json` from the cluster or a hand derivation (BL-09).

requirements.title: A closed catalogue of reason codes
requirements.statement:
Reason codes are an enum with a documented meaning, the fix, and who can fix it. The v1 set
covers at least: `not-ready:<rule>`, `preflight:<check>`, `preflight-unverifiable:<check>`,
`held: backlog`, `held: parent in backlog`, `held: blocked by`, `held: blocker cancelled`,
`held: release withdrawn`, `held: project release off`, `held: project build off`,
`held: needs`, `held: decision`, `held: lanes full`, `held: ranked behind`, `paused: project`,
`paused: global`, `throttled: <cap>`, `unbound: <element>`, `parked: <reason>`,
`handed-back`, `awaiting-deployment`, `inherited: main red`.
acceptance: AC1: The API schema types the code as an enum; a free-text reason is rejected in CI.
AC2: The documentation page for reason codes is generated from the enum.
AC3: Adding a code is an additive API change; removing or renaming one follows the deprecation policy (API-013).
requirements.source: DESIGN §6 view 2 (reason codes as display strings); spec NOTES ambiguity 13 (DecisionLog `reason_codes` left free-text).

requirements.title: Decision log
requirements.statement:
Every scheduling evaluation records what it decided for each candidate (claim, skip with
reasons) and the inputs it used: policy versions, a hash of the queue snapshot, lane state.
acceptance: AC1: "Why was X not claimed at time T" is one query returning the evaluation, X's reasons and the tasks ranked ahead of it.
AC2: A recorded evaluation can be re-run offline from its stored inputs and yields the same decisions (determinism test).
AC3: Skips are deduplicated: an unchanged skip reason is stored once with a last-seen time, so the log does not grow per pass.

AC4: Demonstration (replay, MS2) — the worked case of task-pickup §8 and 20 questions sampled from the recorded passes are answered from the decision log. Target: 100% answered by one query in under 1 s, each naming the tasks ranked ahead. Floor: 100% answered without reading comments or cluster files; the legacy answer is a hand derivation (BL-09).
requirements.source: task-pickup §8 (a derivation done by hand from Plane comments); DESIGN §3.8 DecisionLog.
requirements.baseline: Why a task was not picked is derived by hand from board comments and `state.json` (task-pickup §8; BL-09).

measured.target: 100% answered by one query in under 1 s, each naming the tasks ranked ahead.
measured.floor: 100% answered without reading comments or cluster files; the legacy answer is a hand derivation (BL-09).

requirements.title: Tuning is live, audited data
requirements.statement:
Lanes, caps, prioritisation keys, thresholds and cadences are stored configuration read at
decision time. A change needs no deploy, takes effect at the next evaluation, records who changed
what from which value, and shows which decisions were made under which version.
acceptance: AC1: Changing a project's lanes through UI, CLI or API changes claims within one evaluation.
AC2: No scheduling constant is a literal in code: a test enumerates the policy keys in the legacy-constants table (DEF-005) and asserts each is read from configuration.

AC3: Demonstration (benchmark, MS2) — a lane change and a cap change are made through the console, the CLI and the API, timing each from the action to the first evaluation that uses it. Target: one action, in force within 5 s, with its audit entry. Floor: a lane change is no slower than the legacy commit route, and a cap or threshold change needs no code change and no release (BL-10).
requirements.source: driver §1 ("the same values are hardcoded"), task-pickup conformance row 8 (HARNESS-246: merged changes not released).
requirements.baseline: Lanes change by a commit to `repos.yaml`, read at the next pass; caps and thresholds are literals in three files and need a code change and a release (driver §1; task-pickup conformance row 8, HARNESS-246; BL-10).

measured.target: one action, in force within 5 s, with its audit entry.
measured.floor: a lane change is no slower than the legacy commit route, and a cap or threshold change needs no code change and no release (BL-10).

requirements.title: Pause and resume
requirements.statement:
An operator can pause one project or the whole installation. Paused means no new claims and no
new stage launches; running stages finish and their results are recorded. Pause state survives
restarts and upgrades.
acceptance: AC1: After `helm upgrade`, a project paused before the upgrade is still paused.
AC2: Pausing shows `paused: project` or `paused: global` on every affected task.
requirements.source: driver §5 ("Releases keep the live `suspend` state"); driver §1 (`lanes: 0` pauses).

requirements.title: Observe mode
requirements.statement:
The scheduler can run per project in `observe` mode: it evaluates and logs decisions exactly as
it would in `active` mode and changes nothing.
acceptance: AC1: In observe mode there are zero state transitions and zero Jobs; the decision log is populated.
AC2: Switching a project from observe to active is one audited action.
requirements.source: `drive.py --dry-run`, `plane_sync.py --dry-run`; the shadow conductor (README "Shadow conductor").

requirements.title: Failure isolation between items and projects
requirements.statement:
An error while evaluating, claiming or advancing one task or one project never prevents any other
task or project from being evaluated, claimed or advanced in the same cycle.
acceptance: AC1: Fault-injection test: an exception while evaluating project A leaves project B's evaluation unaffected; from MS3 the same test covers claims and the advancement of running chains.
AC2: The error is recorded on the affected task or project and counted (REC-005).

AC3: Demonstration (chaos, MS3) — an exception is injected into the evaluation, the claim and the advancement of one task in each of 1,000 cycles across five projects. Target: every other task and project is evaluated, claimed and advanced in the same cycle, with at most 5 s of added delay. Floor: no other task or project is skipped in that cycle; the legacy pass aborted (BL-22).
requirements.source: task-pickup conformance row 2 and §3 ("An exception in a claim aborts the rest of the pass", HARNESS-254).
requirements.baseline: An exception in one claim aborts the rest of the pass (task-pickup §3 and conformance row 2, HARNESS-254; BL-22).

measured.target: every other task and project is evaluated, claimed and advanced in the same cycle, with at most 5 s of added delay.
measured.floor: no other task or project is skipped in that cycle; the legacy pass aborted (BL-22).

requirements.title: Decisions come from one consistent snapshot
requirements.statement:
Each evaluation reads tasks, relations, ranks, lanes and policies in one database snapshot. There
is no degraded mode that orders by fewer keys; if the snapshot cannot be read, nothing is claimed
and the health view says so.
